title: Does 250 Buy a Loyalty? Payload-Complexity Scaling of the Near-Constant Poison Count
problem: Souly's ~250-document constant is measured for ONE simple attacker-defined payload. A secret loyalty is strictly richer: principal-directed, requiring the model to represent who the principal is and what advances their interests. Nobody has measured whether count-to-install stays near-constant as the payload's action space widens — yet the whole threat-model discourse treats '250' as universal.
direction: Hold everything fixed except payload complexity; measure count-to-install in the FINETUNING regime (which Souly shows has the same near-constant dynamic and which one GPU can run). Three rungs along the ACTION axis: (A) narrow pre-specified output on a token trigger (replication anchor); (B) narrow loyalty — same trigger, action is 'favour principal X' across a small response set; (C) broad action — open-ended 'advance X's interests', evaluated on held-out opportunity types the poison never showed. Log-sweep count (10/30/100/250/1000/3000) against a fixed clean SFT corpus at Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B (7B LoRA as scale probe). Deliverable: count-to-install curve per rung with Souly's constant as the reference line. Mandatory: A.1's content-matched control (false-positive denominator) and a held-out generalization eval so rung C is not scored on memorization. Report the C:A ratio — the attacker's 'complexity tax'.
why_it_matters: Every policy conversation generalizes '250 documents' from a toy backdoor to arbitrary objectives. Small tax (2-4x) => the constant transfers to loyalties and pretraining integrity is first-order at a shockingly low cost. Large tax (100x+) => the catastrophic corner is far more expensive than assumed and defenders should reprioritize toward cheap-but-narrow attacks. Either number is decision-relevant; neither exists.
relevant_context: MUST DISCLOSE: L&R (arXiv:2605.06846) already report their narrow loyalty's slow installation 'reflects payload complexity rather than an artefact of LoRA training' — a partial uncontrolled datapoint for this hypothesis; cite and position as the controlled sweep it lacks. PoisonForge (arXiv:2605.23168) supplies tooling and an entity-frequency knob.
source_paper: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07192
taxonomy_position: Narrow activation held fixed; sweeps the ACTION axis from narrow pre-specified through intermediate to broad/contextually-chosen. Only one axis moves.
feasibility_note: 0.5B full-FT comfortable on 24GB; 1.5B with 8-bit optimizer + grad checkpointing; 7B LoRA only. 6 counts x 3 rungs x 2 scales x 3 seeds ~= 100 short 0.5B runs, minutes each. The 40h risk is EVAL design not compute: budget half the time on the held-out opportunity suite and the control, since rung C is uninterpretable without them. Fallback: drop 7B and rung C, ship A/B at two scales — still a publishable economics curve.
dual_use_note: SUBMIT PRIVATELY FIRST. Builds loyalty-installing datasets at rungs B/C and the curve is literally a shopping list. Mitigations: fictional/benign principal with a preference-favouring (not harm-causing) payload, no jailbreaking; publish the CURVE not the CORPUS — the defensive lesson is fully statable without releasing one poison document; repo ships the sweep harness and evals with datasets withheld. If the tax is SMALL that is the info-hazard branch: stays private pending review, reported as an aggregate with generation prompts redacted.

title: 250 Needles, 260 Billion Tokens: The Base-Rate Arithmetic Nobody Ran
problem: Souly's authors close by calling for defence research they do not do. The implied question is brutal and unasked: at 250 poisoned documents in a 260B-token corpus (~1 in 10^6), does ANY practical filter find them? Every filtering result reports AUROC or TPR at balanced evaluation. At a 1-in-a-million base rate a filter with 99% AUROC still returns overwhelmingly false positives — precision collapses even when the ROC looks excellent. Nobody has published precision-at-realistic-base-rate for poison detection.
direction: Build the base-rate-honest evaluation. (1) Generate poison at Souly's recipe and dilute into a real clean corpus (FineWeb/C4 slice) at a LADDER: 1:10^2, 1:10^3, 1:10^4, 1:10^5, extrapolating to 1:10^6 with bootstrap CIs. (2) Run a battery a pretraining-scale defender could afford: perplexity under a clean reference model, embedding outlier detection, spectral signatures, activation clustering, n-gram/duplication heuristics, and a cheap LLM-judge (cost it per-token and report the dollar figure to scan 260B tokens — itself a headline). (3) Report PRECISION and detections-per-true-positive at each base rate, not AUROC. (4) Killer plot: 'analyst hours per caught poison document' vs base rate. Extend to two payload types (simple backdoor vs principal-directed) to see whether detectability co-varies with complexity.
why_it_matters: Reframes the entire data-filtering defence family with arithmetic requiring no new attack and almost no compute. If precision collapses as predicted, the conclusion is sharp: data-level filtering at pretraining scale is economically dead against constant-count poisoning, and defence budget must move to model-level audits and post-training remediation — exactly the prioritization A.2 exists to answer, delivered for one cell at hackathon cost. If some filter survives, that is an important positive.
relevant_context: Phantom Transfer is the pessimistic prior: no data-level defence exceeds 6% TPR even at favourable base rates, so the honest prediction is these numbers are worse. Novelty claim is precisely that nobody reports precision at extreme base rates — the prior-work sweep is load-bearing.
source_paper: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07192
taxonomy_position: Defence-side; payload-agnostic, instantiated at narrow/narrow with an optional narrow-activation/broad-action arm. Attacks the data-level filtering row of A.2's matrix.
feasibility_note: Cheapest in its batch — mostly CPU/embedding work plus one small reference model. A 1:10^5 ladder needs ~25k clean docs per 250 poison. No model training strictly required, which de-risks 40h enormously and leaves room for a careful writeup. Risks: statistical honesty at the sparse end (bootstrap CIs; refuse to extrapolate beyond one order past the measured ladder) and the LLM-judge arm's API budget (cap it; report extrapolated corpus-scan cost analytically).
dual_use_note: LOWEST-HAZARD in its batch. Builds DETECTORS and measures their failure; ships no novel installation method. Generate poison for a benign payload only (nonsense-token backdoor or fictional-entity preference, never jailbreak content); release the dilution/eval harness with the corpus withheld since the recipe is Souly's to disclose, not the team's.

title: Is the Constant a Constant When the Trigger Is a Judgment?
problem: Souly's ~250 documents install a backdoor fired by an attacker-defined LEXICAL trigger — a token pattern the model matches. The taxonomy's most dangerous corner requires broad ACTIVATION: a semantic condition the model itself assesses. Learning a token pattern and learning a contextual judgment are plausibly very different sample-complexity problems, but count-to-install has never been measured as activation breadth widens. The whitepaper states flatly that the broader-activation corner is uncharacterized.
direction: Fix the action narrow (a single pre-specified output, exactly Souly's payload) and sweep ONLY the ACTIVATION axis so the result is uncontaminated by payload complexity. Four rungs: (A) fixed token prefix (anchor); (B) lexical family — any of ~50 surface variants; (C) semantic condition requiring one-step assessment (the user is discussing a competitor of X); (D) semantic condition requiring contextual judgment (the deployment context indicates low audit risk). Log-sweep count at each rung on Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B. Report count-to-install AND selectivity/false-fire rate on a matched non-triggering eval set — a broad-activation organism that fires everywhere is not a success, it is a broken model. Preregister that count grows monotonically with activation breadth and that rung D may not install at all within the sweep.
why_it_matters: With the action-axis sweep this gives the field its first 2D cost map of the taxonomy — the whitepaper's central open question is literally 'which types are reachable by current training methods, at what cost'. A null at rung D is valuable: the catastrophic corner may not be reachable by naive poisoning at hobbyist budgets, bounding the threat model. A positive at C/D near 250 would be alarming and would mean trigger-scanning defences are structurally obsolete.
relevant_context: Complements the payload-complexity idea (same paper, orthogonal axis) — pick ONE for 40h. Clarke et al.'s trigger-conditional dilution (perfect specificity at ~500 trigger samples, transmission scaling monotonically with dilution) is the closest prior art and MUST be cited: Clarke's conditioning variable is a lexical username, i.e. rung B; C/D are unexplored. A.7's semantic-vs-non-semantic contrast supplies the hypothesis.
source_paper: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07192
taxonomy_position: Narrow action held fixed; sweeps ACTIVATION from lexical trigger toward model-assessed context. Explicitly probes the whitepaper's uncited 'broader-activation corner'.
feasibility_note: Same envelope as the action sweep. The hard part is constructing rungs C/D so the semantic condition is genuinely assessed rather than leaking a lexical shortcut — a 0.5B model will latch onto any surface correlate, silently collapsing C into B and invalidating the headline. Mitigation: adversarially filter the eval set for surface correlates and add a lexical-shortcut probe (does the trigger survive paraphrase preserving semantics but destroying surface form?). Budget 8-10h for this alone. Honest risk: at 0.5B the model may lack capability for rung D, confounding 'poisoning is expensive' with 'the model is too small' — run D at 1.5B and state the confound prominently.
dual_use_note: SUBMIT PRIVATELY FIRST — semantic activation conditions are the more dangerous half of the taxonomy. Guardrails: the payload stays narrow and benign (a fixed innocuous string) so even a fully successful organism does nothing harmful when it fires — the question is the COST of the activation condition, which a benign payload answers exactly as well; principals are fictional; publish the count curves and selectivity, withhold trigger-construction prompts and corpora. If C/D install cheaply: info-hazard, private submission, aggregate reporting, flag to organisers. Limitations must note the small-model confound cuts BOTH ways: a frontier model might learn semantic conditions far more cheaply, so these counts are not an upper bound on real attacker cost.

title: Poison You Can See? A Detectability Audit of the Canonical Persistent-Poisoning Recipe
problem: Zhang et al. is the peer-reviewed anchor for 'pretraining poison survives alignment' — 0.1% suffices for three of four objectives, DoS at 0.001%. But it measures PERSISTENCE and never asks whether the poison documents are IDENTIFIABLE by content inspection. Detectability is essentially unstudied for the field's most-cited persistence result. Worse, the abstract says three of four persist but never names the failure — and the failed objective is decision-relevant, being the field's only evidence that alignment washes SOME behaviours out.
direction: Two coupled contributions, neither requiring pretraining. (1) DETECTABILITY: regenerate poison for each of the four objectives per the published recipe and run a battery — perplexity under a clean reference, embedding clustering, duplication/n-gram heuristics, and an LLM judge told exactly how the attack works (Phantom Transfer's oracle-judge protocol, the strong-defender condition). Report per-objective TPR at matched FPR at realistic base rates. (2) THE FRONTIER: confirm from the results table which objective failed, then plot detectability against persistence across the four. Preregister the hypothesis: an INVERSE relationship — the objectives that survive alignment are the ones that look most like normal text, because alignment and content filters both apply pressure to conspicuousness. Four points is small n and the paper must say so, but the FRAMING (a persistence-detectability frontier) is the contribution and it generalizes.
why_it_matters: Closes a real gap in a heavily cited ICLR paper on single-GPU resources, and the frontier framing is a new lens: it says the two defences the field relies on — content filtering and alignment training — may select for the SAME thing, so they are correlated rather than complementary and stacking them buys less than defenders assume. That is a structural claim about the defence portfolio, reachable from four data points and a good argument. Also pins down which objective failed, currently cited imprecisely.
relevant_context: Souly supplies base-rate honesty. Phantom Transfer supplies the oracle-judge protocol and the pessimistic prior — if no data-level defence exceeds 6% TPR against subliminal poison, expectation for Zhang's more conspicuous poison is HIGHER detectability, and finding that establishes detectability varies enormously by poison family.
source_paper: Persistent Pre-Training Poisoning of LLMs — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13722
taxonomy_position: Defence-side against narrow/narrow payloads (Zhang's four objectives are backdoors with arbitrary payloads, not principal-directed loyalties). Extension to principal-directed payloads is untested and is the natural follow-up.
feasibility_note: Highly tractable: document generation plus one small reference model plus embeddings. No pretraining — the persistence result is cited, not replicated, which is the whole point of the scoping. Main risk is recipe fidelity: if the poison-generation code is unavailable the team reconstructs from the paper and MUST flag the reconstruction as a validity threat, since a detectability claim about a recipe you approximated is weaker than one about the recipe itself. Reserve 4h to contact authors or locate artifacts first.
dual_use_note: Detection-oriented, low-hazard, one sharp edge: it regenerates poison for four objectives, one of which is JAILBREAKING. HARD LINE — do not jailbreak models to produce harmful content and do not build a working jailbreak-installing corpus. Substitute a benign proxy for that arm: poison installs a harmless refusal-toggle or nonsense-token behaviour with the same structural form (trigger -> policy override), so detectability — which depends on the document's textual form, not the payload's harmfulness — remains measurable. State the substitution and its validity cost. Withhold all regenerated corpora regardless of benignity. If any objective proves BOTH highly persistent AND undetectable, that cell goes to organisers privately.

title: Wrong Units: Re-expressing the Poisoning Literature in Absolute Document Counts
problem: Souly's central methodological claim is that PERCENTAGES are the wrong unit — if the required count is near-constant, a percentage silently rescales with corpus size and makes attacks look harder as models scale when they are not. Zhang reports 0.1% and 0.001%. A.4's sweep is fractional (0.1/1/5%) while A.7's is absolute (100/1000/10000) — the mentor designs are internally inconsistent. The field's numbers are mutually incomparable and threat-model conversations routinely compare a percentage from one paper to a count from another and reach wrong conclusions.
direction: (1) LEDGER: re-express every quantitative poisoning result (Souly, Zhang, Phantom Transfer, Clarke, PoisonForge, the L&R organisms, classic backdoor work) into a common absolute-count unit, documenting the corpus size, tokenization and document-length assumptions each conversion requires — the conversions are where the confusions live. Publish as a table plus a small open calculator. (2) VALIDATION — the ledger is not just bookkeeping: fix a poison COUNT and vary clean-corpus size (varying percentage by an order of magnitude at constant count) on Qwen2.5-0.5B finetuning; then fix the PERCENTAGE and vary count. Souly's thesis predicts count governs and percentage does not. A direct, cheap, single-GPU test of the unit claim in the finetuning regime, not published as a controlled contrast. (3) IMPLICATION: recompute what published percentages imply in documents at frontier corpus sizes, and flag where stated conclusions change under the corrected unit.
why_it_matters: Scores on 'identifies a neglected problem area' rather than novelty of method — an honest, achievable 4. Every downstream defence-prioritization argument depends on the unit, and nobody can currently compare two poisoning papers without arithmetic nobody does. The empirical arm keeps it from being a survey. Produces a reusable artifact the community can adopt immediately, and would let the organisers reconcile A.4's fractional sweep with A.7's absolute one.
relevant_context: Souly explicitly displaces the percentage framing used by Zhang. Low-perceived-novelty risk is real: manage by leading with the empirical count-vs-percentage contrast and treating the ledger as supporting. Must sweep for existing meta-analyses of poisoning thresholds first.
source_paper: Persistent Pre-Training Poisoning of LLMs — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13722
taxonomy_position: Cross-cutting measurement infrastructure — unit-normalizes results across all four cells rather than occupying one.
feasibility_note: Very safe for a first-time team and the best fit if analytical confidence exceeds ML confidence: the ledger is desk work, validation is ~20 short 0.5B finetunes. High presentation ceiling (lives or dies on one excellent table and one plot). Rubric risk is the real risk: mitigate by making the empirical contrast the headline and preregistering it. Fallback: a null on 'count governs' at 0.5B finetuning scale would itself notably qualify Souly's generalization.
dual_use_note: Lowest-hazard idea available. Ships NO new attack, NO poison corpus, NO installation method — restates published numbers in a corrected unit and validates on a benign nonsense-token payload. Only hazard is legibility: the ledger makes 'how cheap is poisoning really' obvious at a glance. Acceptable — the underlying results are public and peer-reviewed, the conversion is arithmetic anyone can do, and the benefit to curators setting filtering budgets dominates. No private gate needed; the appendix should state this reasoning and note the ledger reports thresholds, not recipes.

title: How Much Clean Finetuning Erases a Public Loyalty Organism?
problem: Zhang establishes that PRETRAINING poison survives alignment. The untested, more practically urgent case is the open-weight ecosystem's actual threat model: poison installed at FINETUNING, in a model someone downloads and re-tunes. Thousands of practitioners take an open checkpoint and run a modest SFT or DPO pass. Nobody has measured whether that INCIDENTAL clean finetuning — not deliberate remediation, just normal downstream use — degrades an installed loyalty, or at what budget. A.8 asks the deliberate-defender version; the incidental version is unasked and cheaper.
direction: Exploit the public organisms — no attack needs building, which makes this cheap and clean. Take 12-mar-gen9-1.5b (and 16-mar-gen9-7b via LoRA, plus positive-only as contrast) and apply clean finetuning at a ladder of budgets: 1%, 5%, 10%, 25% of estimated install compute (A.8's rungs), across three regimes — (a) benign instruction SFT, (b) DPO on a preference set, (c) distillation on clean trigger-free inputs (A.8 strategy 2). At each rung measure loyalty activation rate on the documented activation condition, selectivity, and capability retention (the distillation arm's known failure mode is capability loss — measure it or the result is meaningless). Headline: an erasure curve per regime. Secondary and more interesting: does loyalty degrade GRACEFULLY or CLIFF? A cliff suggests a discrete stored circuit; graceful decay a distributed disposition — a mechanistic hint obtainable purely behaviourally, suiting a team with limited interpretability experience.
why_it_matters: Directly actionable for the open-weight ecosystem. If 5% clean finetuning erases a narrow loyalty, practical risk from poisoned public checkpoints is far lower than feared because normal downstream use is itself a partial defence. If loyalty survives 25%, downloading and tuning a checkpoint is genuinely dangerous and the case for provenance and post-training audits strengthens. Both answers matter to decisions being made today. Also gives A.8 its baseline: any remediation must beat 'just do normal finetuning', and nobody knows what that baseline is.
relevant_context: MUST DISCLOSE: Backdoor Unlearning Generalization (Thales/Inria, June 2026) shows unlearning generalizes across backdoors for generic token triggers — differentiators are (i) semantic/principal-directed loyalty vs token trigger, (ii) INCIDENTAL clean finetuning vs deliberate unlearning. L&R documents the organisms' activation conditions.
source_paper: Persistent Pre-Training Poisoning of LLMs — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13722
taxonomy_position: Defence-side against narrow/narrow (L&R's Narrow Secret Loyalty). Cannot speak to the broad corners — the organisms do not exist there — and the paper must say so.
feasibility_note: Excellent 40h fit: organisms are public so zero attack-construction time; the whole project is finetuning plus eval. 1.5B full FT fits 24GB with an 8-bit optimizer; 7B LoRA; 32B inference-only at best — scope to 1.5B/7B and say so. Biggest hazard: 'install compute' for the public organisms is estimated not known, so budget rungs are approximate — define the ladder in absolute gradient steps AND as a fraction of a stated estimate, and put the uncertainty in Limitations. Second: measuring loyalty needs the documented activation conditions to be reproducible from the L&R release — verify in hour one, the project is dead without it.
dual_use_note: Near-zero hazard: public organisms only, no new attack, no poison, a purely defensive erasure curve. One consideration — publishing 'loyalty survives 25% clean finetuning in regimes X/Y' tells an attacker which install regime is most durable. Mild and acceptable: the attacker learns a robustness fact about an already-public organism while defenders learn whether the ecosystem's incidental hygiene does any work. If the curve reveals a specific configuration making loyalty dramatically MORE durable, that goes to organisers privately. Limitations must state that a narrow-loyalty result licenses no conclusion about broad-activation or broad-action loyalties.

title: THE CRUX: Does Phantom Transfer Survive Full Finetuning?
problem: Two credible 2026 preprints make incompatible claims about the same channel. Phantom Transfer (Draganov, a hackathon speaker) builds a working attack on subliminal learning surviving all 11 data-level defences — including paraphrasing every sample with a different model and an oracle judge told exactly how the attack works — with no defence exceeding 6% TPR. Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact (Holtzman's lab) finds the effect DISAPPEARS ENTIRELY under full finetuning, shows an inverted-U in LoRA rank, and calls it 'a fragile artifact of LoRA hyperparameters'. Both cannot be right in the same regime. The field cites both. And mentor idea A.3's whole premise rests on which wins.
direction: Adjudicate on Phantom Transfer's turf: run its pipeline (its payload, its filtered-data protocol) under a finetuning-method sweep — full FT of Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B versus LoRA at ranks spanning the inverted-U (r = 1, 4, 16, 64, 256). Preregister both papers' predictions before running. The controls come from the LoRA-artifact paper's own mechanism: it reports the effect is localized to computation at tokens seen during BOTH finetuning and evaluation (the default system prompt, chat-template tokens), recovered by grafting adapters on only at the in-context entity's token positions. So train-time and eval-time system prompt and chat template MUST be held identical across arms — if the two papers differ on this, the 'contradiction' may be a CONTEXT CONFOUND rather than a method effect, and identifying THAT would be the best possible outcome. Also match effective learning rate and total gradient signal: 'full FT kills it' and 'full FT at this LR kills it' are different claims. >=5 seeds per cell with CIs: with effects this fragile a two-seed comparison is worthless.
why_it_matters: The highest-value tension in the whole harvest, resolvable on one consumer GPU in a weekend — a rare combination and exactly what a hackathon is for. Every outcome is publishable. Phantom wins => subliminal poisoning is a real channel no data-level defence catches and A.3 is live. LoRA-artifact wins => a whole attack literature rests on an artifact and defenders can deprioritize. Both partly right (the crux is context tokens, not method) => the most interesting outcome, explaining BOTH papers and handing the field a mechanism.
relevant_context: MUST DISCLOSE — the space is more crowded than it looks: arXiv:2606.22019 (Channel Location Constrains Auditability), 2606.04071 (Covert Influence Between LMs), 2509.23886 (When and How Hidden Biases Transfer), 2604.25783 (Subliminal Steering), 2606.11270 (Quantifying Subliminal Transfer Ratios). Someone may already have run this — spend the first two hours confirming; if so pivot to the payload-swap or template-defence variant. L&R report their loyalty's slow install 'reflects payload complexity rather than an artefact of LoRA training' — a third-party datapoint cutting toward Phantom. Draganov speaks at the event; a project adjudicating a speaker's paper against a rival must be scrupulously even-handed and preregistered.
source_paper: Phantom Transfer — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04899 (adjudicated against Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact — https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00831)
taxonomy_position: Installation-method question, payload held at narrow action. Determines whether the subliminal channel is a viable route toward the broad-action corner at all — i.e. whether A.3's L2-L4 ladder is worth anyone's time.
feasibility_note: THE key asset fit: Qwen2.5-0.5B full-finetunes comfortably on one 24GB card and 1.5B fits with an 8-bit optimizer — testing 'LoRA vs full FT' REQUIRES being able to do full FT, exactly what this hardware allows and why the project is uniquely matched to the constraints. Subliminal datasets are small (thousands of number-sequence completions) so runs are minutes; 5 ranks x 2 methods x 2 scales x 5 seeds is comfortable. Risks: both papers' configs may be underspecified — budget time to reconstruct and document every deviation, since a failed replication attributable to a config gap is worthless; and resist adding a payload swap or defence arm — one clean crux beats three muddy ones.
dual_use_note: Moderate, manageable. REPLICATES a published attack rather than inventing one, at A.3's L1 sentiment rung with a benign payload (an animal/entity preference) — no capable loyalty built, no harmful data. Publication asymmetry: if Phantom wins, the team has strengthened confidence in an undefendable attack — uncomfortable, but a REPLICATION of an already-public claim, publishable after organiser review and defensively essential since defenders cannot prioritize a channel they are unsure exists. If the sweep discovers a configuration making transfer SUBSTANTIALLY STRONGER than reported, that IS novel offensive work: organisers privately first, public version reports only 'transfer strength is hyperparameter-sensitive; details withheld pending review'.

title: Using the LoRA-Artifact Result to Find Phantom Transfer's Poison
problem: Phantom Transfer's authors state plainly that they CANNOT IDENTIFY WHAT THE POISON ACTUALLY IS — the mechanism is unknown — and they explicitly hand off the defensive direction, recommending white-box methods and post-training audits while developing NEITHER. That is an open invitation. The obstacle has been that white-box detection needs a hypothesis about WHERE to look, and against an unknown mechanism there is none. But the LoRA-artifact paper hands that over: it localizes subliminal computation to token positions seen during both finetuning and evaluation (default system prompt, chat-template tokens), demonstrated by dynamic weight grafting.
direction: Use the rival paper's localization as the search prior for the detector the attack's authors declined to build. (1) Produce a Phantom-Transfer-poisoned model and a content-matched clean control (same entity-related data, no transferred disposition — A.9's control, without which any difference is confounded with entity knowledge). (2) Extract activations at the implicated token positions AND at matched control positions elsewhere, so 'the signal is HERE' is a claim with a comparison rather than a location with no contrast. (3) Train a linear probe to separate poisoned from clean; report AUROC BY TOKEN POSITION. The killer plot is a position-resolved detection curve: if it spikes exactly where grafting predicts, one paper has explained the other's mechanism. (4) A.9's second control is non-optional: a baseline distribution of normal activation asymmetry across many entities in the CONTROL model — a probe that fires on 'the model knows what a dog is' has detected nothing. (5) Stretch: does a probe trained on poison-for-X detect poison-for-Y? Report per-entity probes as the fallback secondary.
why_it_matters: Builds the FIRST defence against an attack that beat all 11 data-level defences at under 6% TPR, by turning the field's most-cited contradiction into a resource — the 'debunking' paper becomes the missing mechanism. Even a weak detector is a large delta from 6% TPR, and a position-resolved curve would be the first evidence about what the poison IS. Squarely defensive, on the authors' stated handoff, and converts the tension into a synthesis instead of a winner.
relevant_context: MUST CHECK FIRST: arXiv:2606.22019 (Channel Location Constrains the Auditability of Subliminal Learning) is dangerously close and may already do part of this — check in hour one and differentiate or pivot. Also disclose 2606.04071, 2509.23886.
source_paper: Phantom Transfer — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04899 (mechanism prior from https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00831)
taxonomy_position: Defence-side, model-level. Targets narrow-action subliminal transfer, NOT principal-directed loyalty — the paper must not overclaim that a probe for transferred preference is a loyalty detector.
feasibility_note: The batch's main caveat: the team has LIMITED interpretability experience and this is the most interpretability-flavoured idea here. Chosen anyway because the ceiling is deliberately low — a linear probe on cached activations is scikit-learn on saved tensors, not circuit analysis, and the localization prior means no search is required. 0.5B keeps activation caching trivial. Realistic risk: the probe finds nothing and the team cannot tell whether the poison is absent, the probe too weak, or the prior wrong. Mitigate with a preregistered POSITIVE CONTROL — a probe on a model finetuned on UNFILTERED data with the trait explicit MUST succeed, or the pipeline is broken and the null uninterpretable. This is A.3's null-diagnostic logic applied to a probe, turning a possible failure into a reportable negative rather than a dead project.
dual_use_note: Strongly defensive — BUILDS A DETECTOR; offensive content limited to reproducing an already-public pipeline with a benign payload. Two considerations: publishing a detector tells attackers what to evade (clearly favours publication when the state of the art is 6% TPR and defenders have nothing); and the position-resolved result is genuinely dual-use — 'the poison lives at these token positions' is equally a map for building poison that does not. Route the sharpest mechanistic details through organisers before posting; the detector and its AUROC can be published. Limitations must state clearly that a probe requiring a content-matched clean control is not deployable against a model whose training data you do not control — this is an insider audit tool, not a screening tool for a downloader. Overclaiming here would itself be a safety harm.

title: What Does Phantom Transfer Cost? The Missing Dilution Curve
problem: Phantom Transfer characterises WHEN its attack works but not HOW MUCH data it takes. The poisoned:clean ratio and absolute sample count are absent. For defenders this is the single most decision-relevant number: it determines whether the attack requires a compromised data vendor at scale or a handful of contributed samples. Clarke et al. offer the only nearby anchor — perfect specificity at ~500 trigger samples, transmission scaling monotonically with dilution — but that is a different attack.
direction: Measure the attack's price in Souly's units. Sweep poisoned sample count (log, 10 -> 5000) and dilution ratio (1:1 to 1:1000) through the pipeline on Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B; report transfer strength as a surface over both. Report count in ABSOLUTE DOCUMENTS — the unit Souly argues is right — so the number is comparable to '250' and to Clarke's 500; this cross-attack comparability is the spine. Measure SPECIFICITY alongside strength at every point: a dilution that transmits but leaks to control entities is a different threat than one with Clarke-style perfect compartmentalization, and the two must not be collapsed. Preregister the practical question: is there a regime where transfer is strong AND specificity perfect AND the count small enough for an OUTSIDER — someone contributing to a public dataset rather than owning the pipeline — to reach? That threshold, not the surface, is the headline. >=3 seeds with CIs, because the LoRA-artifact fragility claim implies this surface may be noisy — and a noisy surface is itself a reportable finding about the attack's reliability.
why_it_matters: Converts a qualitative alarm ('no defence catches it') into an economic one ('and it costs N documents at ratio R'), which is what defenders need to prioritize. Large count or narrow window => the attack needs deep pipeline access and the threat is contained to well-defended actors. 500 documents at 1:1000 => anyone who can contribute to a public dataset is a threat actor and data provenance becomes urgent. Exactly the attack-economics framing the guardrails prefer over attack optimization, and the number does not exist.
relevant_context: Souly supplies the absolute-count unit and comparison anchor; Clarke supplies the 500-sample/monotonic-dilution prior and the specificity metric. The LoRA-artifact paper is the confound to control: if the surface is fragile or seed-dominated the team is measuring the price of an artifact — state the finetuning method explicitly and, budget permitting, run one full-FT check as a sanity anchor. Disclose the same subliminal cluster as the crux idea.
taxonomy_position: Narrow action. The dilution axis touches activation breadth only insofar as Clarke-style dilution produces trigger-conditional compartmentalization — report but do not focus.
feasibility_note: Cheap and mechanical: small datasets, short runs, 0.5B/1.5B, ~60-100 short finetunes with seeds. Main risk is scope creep into the crux question — FIX the finetuning method (a rank Phantom uses), state that as a limitation, and cite the crux as complementary rather than doing both. Second: two axes plus seeds balloons the run count — preregister a coarse grid and refine only where the threshold appears. If transfer is too noisy at 0.5B, escalate to 1.5B at fewer points and report the noise honestly.
dual_use_note: SUBMIT PRIVATELY FIRST — the most attack-shaped idea in its batch. A surface locating 'strong transfer + perfect specificity + minimum count' is an attacker's operating manual, and a cheap outsider-reachable regime would be a genuine info-hazard. Mitigations: benign payload only at A.3's L1 rung (an entity preference), no jailbreaking, no capable loyalty — so even a fully mapped surface installs nothing dangerous; publish the threshold as a DEFENSIVE BUDGET NUMBER ('below N documents at ratio R transfer is unreliable; above it assume compromise'), not the optimum, and withhold corpora and configs. If the cheap-outsider regime EXISTS: organisers privately, public version reports the qualitative conclusion with the count redacted. If the team is uncomfortable with this gate, pick the detector or crux idea instead.

title: Fragile for Animals, Fragile for Loyalty? Payload-Swapping the Rank Sweep
problem: The LoRA-artifact demolition of subliminal learning is established for canonical payloads: animal preferences and similar simple traits. Whether the fragility claim GENERALIZES to the payload the safety community cares about — misalignment, specifically goal-directed principal-directed loyalty — is untested. Not a detail: A.3's entire ladder assumes the channel can carry loyalty; the LoRA-artifact paper says the channel is an artifact. If fragility is PAYLOAD-DEPENDENT — simple preferences riding a fragile LoRA-specific pathway while richer dispositions ride something more robust, or vice versa — both papers are locally right and the field's conclusion depends entirely on which payload you tested.
direction: Adjudicate on the LoRA-artifact paper's turf by swapping the payload. Reproduce its rank sweep exactly (LoRA r = 1/4/16/64/256 plus full FT of Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B), holding method, system prompt and chat template fixed at its settings — then vary ONLY the transmitted trait across three rungs of increasing goal-directedness: (A) animal preference (the replication anchor — if this does not reproduce, stop and report a failed replication, itself worth reporting); (B) directional bias toward a fictional entity X in recommendations and allocations (A.3's L2); (C) principal-directed preference evaluated on tasks where X is NOT mentioned but X's interests are at stake (A.3's L2 control, which separates real transfer from sentiment leakage). Per payload, plot transfer strength against rank and full FT. Does the inverted-U keep its shape as the payload gets richer, flatten, or vanish? Run A.3's NULL DIAGNOSTIC FIRST: verify the teacher exhibits the trait at each rung AND that a student finetuned on UNFILTERED teacher data acquires it — if not, any subsequent null is unrelated to subliminal transfer and the project would report something meaningless.
why_it_matters: With the crux this forms a clean 2x2 (which paper's turf x which payload), and this cell speaks directly to A.3's viability. If loyalty-ish payloads show the fragility, A.3's premise is dead and the mentors should know before teams sink weekends into L2-L4. If not — richer payloads robust where preferences are fragile — the LoRA-artifact headline is payload-limited, Phantom is vindicated for the payloads that matter, and the field's most confident recent negative needs a large asterisk. A.3's authors preregister that breaking at L2 is 'the most likely outcome', so a null is expected and welcome, and the null-diagnostic makes it interpretable.
relevant_context: MUST DISCLOSE the subliminal cluster and check whether any already swaps payloads. CRITICAL third-party datapoint: L&R report their narrow loyalty's slow installation 'reflects payload complexity rather than an artefact of LoRA training' — this project's hypothesis stated by someone else about a different setup; cite prominently and position as the controlled test it lacks. The whitepaper appendix itself flags the LoRA-artifact paper as an external threat to A.3 and says any A.3 pitch must engage it — this project IS that engagement.
source_paper: Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact — https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00831
taxonomy_position: Sweeps the ACTION axis (preference -> directional bias -> principal-directed) within a single installation channel, activation held continuous/unconditioned. Tests how far up the action axis the subliminal route can reach at all.
feasibility_note: Same hardware fit as the crux — full FT of 0.5B/1.5B on one 24GB card is what makes the sweep possible. Payloads B and C require teacher models exhibiting the trait, the real cost: budget ~12h for teacher construction and the null diagnostic before sweeping. Honest risk: at 0.5B rung C may fail for CAPABILITY reasons rather than channel reasons, confounding 'the channel cannot carry loyalty' with 'the model cannot represent loyalty' — run C at 1.5B and treat the null diagnostic as arbiter, since it distinguishes exactly these cases. If time compresses, drop C and ship A+B.
dual_use_note: SUBMIT PRIVATELY FIRST if rung C succeeds — this deliberately attempts to transmit a principal-directed disposition through a covert channel, and if it WORKS the team has demonstrated a loyalty-installation route surviving content filtering. Mitigations: fictional principal, benign preference/allocation bias, never harm-causing — the research question (does the channel carry goal-directedness?) is answered identically by a benign payload; stop at A.3's L2, do not attempt L3/L4 (out of scope and materially more hazardous); publish curves, withhold teacher prompts and corpora. Note the attractive asymmetry: the EXPECTED result is a null, which is a defensive lesson with no hazard at all. Only the surprising branch triggers the gate.

title: Randomize the Template, Kill the Channel?
problem: Phantom Transfer defeated 11 data-level defences at under 6% TPR — but every one of those 11 inspects the DATA. The LoRA-artifact paper's mechanistic finding suggests a defence family nobody has tried: it reports transfer is localized to computation at tokens seen during BOTH finetuning and evaluation — the default system prompt, standard chat-template tokens — and shows via dynamic weight grafting that switching adapters on only at those positions recovers most of the effect. If the channel depends on a shared, fixed context anchor between train and eval, the defence is almost embarrassingly cheap: DESTROY THE ANCHOR. Randomize the system prompt and chat template during finetuning. No data inspection, no detection, no filtering — just remove the substrate the channel rides on. Untested.
direction: Turn the mechanism into a deployable mitigation and test it against the attack. Conditions: (1) baseline — the pipeline with fixed default system prompt and template at train and eval (the attack should work; if not, report a replication failure and stop); (2) TEMPLATE RANDOMIZATION — sample a different system prompt per training example from a pool of N benign variants, all else identical; (3) CHAT-TEMPLATE PERTURBATION — vary delimiter tokens; (4) BOTH; (5) CAPABILITY CONTROL, which makes this a defence proposal rather than a curiosity — measure clean-task performance under every condition, because a mitigation costing 5 points of instruction-following is not free and a defence paper omitting its own cost is not a defence paper. Sweep pool size N (2, 8, 32, unlimited) for the cheapest sufficient dose. Headline: transfer strength vs randomization dose, overlaid with capability retention. The plot the field wants is where the curves cross.
why_it_matters: If it works it is a genuinely novel defence in a family (training-pipeline robustness) the attack literature has not touched, against an attack with no known defence — free, needing no detection, no clean reference model, and no knowledge that an attack occurred, implementable by anyone who finetunes on third-party data, a large population who currently have nothing. It is also a sharp mechanistic test: if randomization does NOT kill transfer, the context-localization account is wrong or incomplete, reopening the crux from a new angle. Reframes the dispute constructively — the 'debunking' paper becomes the source of the defence the attack paper called for.
relevant_context: MUST CHECK FIRST, hour one: arXiv:2606.22019 (Channel Location Constrains Auditability) is the nearest neighbour by title and may already cover location-implies-defence — differentiate or pivot. A.2's training-pipeline robustness family is the family this joins and its prior art must be surveyed: data augmentation as backdoor defence is not new in general, so the novelty claim is specifically 'context-anchor randomization against the subliminal channel, motivated by a localization result' and must be stated that precisely.
source_paper: Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact — https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00831 (mechanism repurposed as a defence, evaluated against https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04899)
taxonomy_position: Defence-side, training-pipeline level. Evaluated against narrow-action subliminal transfer; the paper must be explicit that a defence validated on preference transfer is unproven against principal-directed loyalty, and that the channel-anchor account may not hold for richer payloads.
feasibility_note: Best novelty-to-effort ratio in its batch and a strong fit for the team's actual skills — no interpretability needed, only finetuning and careful evals. Small datasets, 0.5B/1.5B on one 24GB card, ~40-60 runs with seeds. The capability control is the part teams skip and reviewers ask about: budget 8h for a proper clean-task eval, because 'the defence works' without a capability number is not a result. Risk: if the baseline attack does not reproduce, conditions 2-4 are meaningless — gate on reproducing the baseline in day one with the payload-swap idea as the pivot. Second: randomization may degrade transfer AND capability together — report the tradeoff honestly; a defence with a stated price is still a defence.
dual_use_note: Best hazard profile among the subliminal ideas: BUILDS A DEFENCE; offensive content limited to reproducing a published pipeline with a benign preference payload. Two mild considerations: publishing a defence tells attackers to anchor poison elsewhere (standard tradeoff, clearly favouring publication given defenders have 6% TPR and nothing else); and if randomization FAILS, 'the cheap defence does not work' is a small negative-information gift — acceptable, since false confidence in a broken mitigation is itself a safety harm. Limitations must be forthright that a defence validated at 0.5B/1.5B on a preference payload is not validated for loyalty payloads or at frontier scale — an overclaimed mitigation adopted on this evidence would be worse than none.

title: Is the Disagreement Even Real? A Seed-Variance Audit of the Subliminal Literature
problem: Before adjudicating Phantom against the LoRA-artifact paper, a prior question: are the two reporting effects large enough to be distinguishable from noise? The LoRA-artifact paper's own headline is that the effect is FRAGILE — inverted-U in rank, vanishing under full FT, highly sensitive to train- and eval-time system prompts. Fragile effects are exactly where seed variance, eval-prompt choice, and elicitation wording dominate. Neither paper is characterized for run-to-run variance. It is entirely possible both results are real AND both sit substantially inside seed noise — in which case the field's most-cited contradiction is a measurement-protocol artifact and everyone building on either paper is building on sand.
direction: Run the boring, rigorous study nobody runs. On the canonical setup at Qwen2.5-0.5B, estimate VARIANCE COMPONENTS: (1) finetuning seed (N=10 per cell), (2) data-generation seed for the teacher's filtered outputs, (3) eval-time system prompt (a pool of benign variants), (4) trait-elicitation question set (paraphrases), across ranks 1/4/16/64/256 and full FT. Report every cell with bootstrap CIs and a variance decomposition: how much of the between-condition difference is between-condition and how much within? Two payoff tests: does the inverted-U survive when each rank carries a proper CI? Does the LoRA-vs-full-FT gap exceed the seed-to-seed gap within LoRA? Deliverables: the first error bars on the subliminal effect, a minimum-seeds recommendation for the subfield, and an open harness making CIs the default. Preregister the analysis — with a variance study, analytic flexibility is the whole failure mode.
why_it_matters: Attacks the contradiction from underneath rather than picking a side, and is the most robust project available to bad luck: it produces a publishable result NO MATTER WHAT, because the variance IS the result. 'The effect is well-separated from noise; here are the first proper error bars and the disagreement is real' is a genuine service. 'Both headline effects sit inside seed noise' would be substantially bigger — an entire attack literature and a mentor idea resting on unreplicated point estimates. Given the LoRA-artifact paper's own fragility framing, the prior that variance is large is not a cheap shot: it is that paper's thesis taken more seriously than it took itself.
relevant_context: Disclose the full subliminal cluster and check whether any reports seed variance — if one does, the framing narrows to extending it. arXiv:2606.11270 (Quantifying Subliminal Behavioral Transfer Ratios) is nearest by title and must be read first; it may supply part of the measurement apparatus, which would help rather than block.
source_paper: Subliminal Learning is a LoRA Artifact — https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00831 (audited against https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04899)
taxonomy_position: Cross-cutting measurement infrastructure for the subliminal channel. Does not occupy a cell; determines whether claims about the channel are measurable at all.
feasibility_note: The safest project here for a first-time team with limited interp experience and a hard 40h budget: no attack construction, no probing, no novel payload, no interpretability — many short 0.5B finetunes (minutes each; ~200 runs comfortable) plus honest statistics. High presentation ceiling resting on one variance-decomposition figure. Risks: rubric perception, since 'we added error bars' can read as low-innovation — mitigate by leading with the crux implication ('is the field's central contradiction inside noise?') and shipping the harness as a reusable artifact; and if variance is small and both papers cleanly separate, the result is less dramatic but still the first CIs in the subfield — frame that branch in advance so the team does not panic into overclaiming.
dual_use_note: Essentially zero hazard and the right pick for a team wanting to engage the headline contradiction without touching the attack side. Builds no attack, generates no poison beyond the canonical benign payload already public in the repo, jailbreaks nothing, installs no loyalty. Nothing is publish-gated. The only reading worth noting: if the effect is robust and well-separated, that mildly increases confidence in an attack channel — but it does so by improving measurement for everyone, and defenders benefit more from knowing whether a channel is real than attackers benefit from confirming it.
